summary: Presents the motivation and background behind the IESG recommendation to the IAB for a single common IGP for the IP parts of the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Different networks used different ways to share road maps inside themselves. This paper explains why they should all pick one common way.

subtitle: The IESG's recommendation that all IP routers should support OSPF as their common interior gateway protocol.

tldr.problem: By 1991, two modern link-state routing protocols had been developed: OSPF (designed for IP alone) and Integrated IS-IS (designed for both IP and OSI). With both available as standards, vendors and operators lacked clear guidance on which protocol to standardize on internally within their networks, potentially fragmenting the market.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG evaluated both protocols based on implementation maturity, operational experience, and interoperability testing. OSPF had advanced to Draft Internet Standard status with proven multi-vendor interoperation and several operational deployments. Integrated IS-IS was still at Proposed status with limited operational evidence.
tldr.outcome: The IESG recommended OSPF as the common IGP for IP, with the goal that all router vendors would make it a 'MUST IMPLEMENT' requirement. This provided vendor interoperability without prohibiting other protocols where technically justified.

facts.label: OSPF operational status in 1991
facts.value: Draft Internet Standard with multi-vendor interop demonstrated

facts.label: Integrated IS-IS status in 1991
facts.value: Proposed Internet Standard with limited operational evidence

today: RFC 1371 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. OSPF became the dominant IGP in IP networks, and the recommendation to make it a 'MUST IMPLEMENT' requirement shaped router vendor products for decades. Integrated IS-IS saw adoption in some carrier networks but remained less common. The approach of recommending a common protocol without mandating its use became a template for future Internet standardization efforts.

sections.title: The Need for a Common Routing Protocol
sections.content:
An Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) is the routing protocol used within a single administrative domain (an Autonomous System). By 1992, two modern, sophisticated link-state routing protocols had been standardized. The Internet Architecture supports multiple standard protocols coexisting, but operators faced a practical problem: when buying routers from different vendors to use within one network, would they all speak the same IGP?

By 'common', the RFC means ubiquitously available—that users and network operators could expect any router from any vendor to support the protocol. This is essential because if vendor A routers only support protocol X and vendor B routers only support protocol Y, an operator cannot mix vendors in the same network. The IESG recognized both OSPF and Integrated IS-IS as legitimate standardized protocols, but recommended one as the common IGP to enable vendor interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: When you bought routers from different companies for your network, you needed them all to speak the same routing language. The IESG had to pick one language that all router makers would support.

sections.title: OSPF and Integrated IS-IS
sections.content:
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link-state routing protocol designed solely for IP networks. Integrated IS-IS is based on the OSI IS-IS protocol but enhanced to support both IP and OSI CLNP simultaneously. Both are modern Dijkstra-algorithm-based protocols with comparable capabilities and significant cooperation between their development communities.

The key difference: OSPF is IP-only, while Integrated IS-IS supports dual-protocol operation. This distinction became important because the Internet was moving toward supporting both TCP/IP and OSI protocols. For pure IP networks (the common case in 1992), both protocols were suitable. For mixed IP/CLNP networks, Integrated IS-IS offered an advantage if 'integrated routing' was desired—using one protocol for both suites instead of running two separate routing protocols ('Ships in the Night').
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF is made just for IP networks. Integrated IS-IS is based on an OSI standard but was modified to handle both IP and OSI at the same time. Picking one would help routers understand each other.

sections.title: Multi-Protocol Topologies and Integration Options
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that the future Internet would contain diverse protocol environments. Four scenarios were identified: pure IP networks (any IGP works), pure CLNP networks (OSI IS-IS works), dual IP/CLNP networks with a common topology (one topology for both suites—operators could use separate routing protocols or integrated routing), and dual networks with differing topologies (separate protocols required).

For common-topology dual networks, 'Ships in the Night' means running OSPF for IP routes and a separate OSI IS-IS process for CLNP routes—they coexist on the same hardware without interacting. Integrated routing uses Integrated IS-IS for both. The RFC notes that Ships in the Night is most widely used in 1992, but Integrated IS-IS has potential advantages in reducing resource use. The IESG chose not to mandate a preference, but recommended implementing Integrated IS-IS to gather operational experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks would run both IP and OSI. They could either have separate routing languages for each (ships in the night) or use one language that speaks both. The IESG said to try both and see what works.

sections.title: The OSPF Recommendation
sections.content:
Based on operational evidence, the IESG recommended OSPF as the common IGP for the IP portions of the Internet. By 1991, OSPF had been tested extensively: all features had been tested (though not all were used in operational networks), it had operated successfully in several networks with 10–30 routers, and interoperation among routers from multiple vendors had been demonstrated at organized interoperability bakeoffs.

The recommendation was that the IETF Router Requirements Working Group specify OSPF as 'MUST IMPLEMENT' in the Router Requirements document. This does not mandate that operators use OSPF—they remain free to use any protocol—but ensures that all router vendors implement it, allowing interoperation if an operator chooses to deploy it. The recommendation deliberately does not take a position on which protocol is technically superior, nor does it prevent vendors from supporting other protocols or operators from using alternatives where justified.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF had proven itself in tests and real networks with routers from different makers. So the IESG said: 'all router makers should build in OSPF so customers can mix and match routers if they want to.'
